measurements.counting_rule: [normalization:visible-prose/1] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, and you'll in the author-visible prose (recognizable quotations excluded).

[normalization:visible-prose/1] Count case-sensitive whole-word tokens we, We, us, our, Our, ours, Ours, and the listed contracted we forms in the author-visible prose (recognizable quotations excluded); uppercase US is excluded.

[normalization:visible-prose/1] Count whole-word n't, 're, 've, 'll, 'd, and 'm forms plus 's only for the closed elision hosts it, that, there, here, who, what, where, when, how, why, he, she, let, one, nothing, everything, something, somebody, nobody, and this; possessive 's is excluded.

[normalization:visible-prose/1] Count case-insensitive whole phrases do not, does not, did not, is not, are not, was not, were not, cannot, could not, would not, should not, will not, have not, has not, and had not in the author-visible prose (recognizable quotations excluded).

[normalization:visible-prose/1] Count only the case-insensitive whole-word profanity and vulgarity forms enumerated by the prose-author profanity rule; coined words containing a rude root are excluded.
[normalization:visible-prose/1] Count case-insensitive whole-word tokens I, me, my, mine, and myself in the author-visible prose (recognizable quotations excluded).
[normalization:visible-prose/1] Count every literal question-mark character in the author-visible prose (recognizable quotations excluded).
[normalization:visible-prose/1] Count each non-nested pair of round brackets whose contents stay on one line in the author-visible prose (recognizable quotations excluded).
[normalization:visible-prose/1] Count every literal em-dash character in the author-visible prose (recognizable quotations excluded).
[normalization:visible-prose/1] Count every literal en-dash character in the author-visible prose (recognizable quotations excluded).

observations.description: In these institutional advocacy articles, first-person plural presents an organizational position or reporting action. The writing self appears as a participant in public debate rather than through personal autobiography.

citations.quote: We hope the Senate promptly rejects this bill.
We reached out to Patronscan with questions regarding their practices and their views on California ID law.

observations.description: Direct reader address appears in conditional closing invitations, identifying the relevant audience before suggesting participation.

citations.quote: If you are a California resident and want to speak out about A.B. 412, you can find and contact your legislators
If you are a California resident and interested in speaking out about this bill, you can find and contact your representatives

observations.description: Contractions keep explanatory passages conversational; full negative forms also appear in emphatic judgments. Negation often supplies a brief rebuttal or distinguishes a stated purpose from the author's account of its effects.

citations.quote: It’s not merely hypothetical. It’s what happens when speech becomes a legal risk.
KOSA will not make kids safer.
The bill is premised on the idea that copyright owners currently don’t have good remedies if they’re mistreated by AI companies. That simply isn’t true.
But A.B. 412 does not strike the right balance.

observations.description: Concessions acknowledge an understandable goal or a revision before a pivot restates the objection. They appear near the start of an argument or when assessing amendments.

citations.quote: Transparency in AI development is a laudable goal. But A.B. 412 failed to offer a fair or effective path to get there.
That change does address some of the broadest concerns raised about the original proposal, though some questions about the bill’s reach remain.

observations.description: Modal verbs qualify particular scenarios and interpretations inside otherwise assertive arguments. Possible responses and boundary cases receive narrower wording than the surrounding conclusions.

citations.quote: Some providers might ask for government-issued identification.
As conversational AI becomes more emotionally responsive, a customer service chatbot’s efforts to empathize may sweep it within the bill’s definition.

observations.description: Limited to the KIDS Act piece, clustered rhetorical questions turn abstract content categories into everyday situations. The questions invite the reader to test the proposed boundaries through concrete examples.

citations.quote: Can teens discuss addiction and recovery? Can a 15-year-old post that she’s worried she has a friend who is drinking too much? Can they seek advice about a parent’s gambling problem, or get help if they or a family member have been scammed? Can they participate in harm-reduction communities or discuss substance abuse treatment?

observations.description: Attribution identifies whose position or response is being reported before developing the argument. Organizational sources and the subject's own response provide documentary grounding; their quoted language is not evidence of the author's phrasing.

citations.quote: Supporters note that PACER currently collects more than $150 million annually in fees from the public, despite court records being public documents.
We reached out to Patronscan with questions regarding their practices and their views on California ID law.

observations.description: Dashes insert brief emphasis or introduce a consequence within a sentence. This is observable in the supplied publication text; authorship of dash choice and spacing is unverified, so these typographic details should not be treated as settled personal preferences.

citations.quote: Sponsors are claiming—again—that the latest version won’t censor online content.
When states try to rewrite the rules, they create confusion—and more litigation that doesn’t help anyone.

observations.description: Compact metaphors translate administrative or technical arrangements into familiar physical objects. They sit within explanation, making an asserted limitation or risk easier to picture without becoming extended allegories.

citations.quote: The registration system is a cumbersome beast at best–neither machine-readable nor accessible, it’s more like a card catalog than a database
Once Congress requires AI companies to create a permanent, centralized record of teen AI conversations for parental review, that will be a valuable vault of extremely personal information.

observations.description: Openings establish a legislative development and quickly introduce an evaluative turn. These are dated publication openings, not current status reports; relative time expressions belong to their original publication context.

citations.quote: The Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA) is back in the Senate. Sponsors are claiming—again—that the latest version won’t censor online content. It isn’t true.
The legislation is presented as a technical reorganization of some government agencies, but it’s much more than that.

observations.description: Closings often compress the argument into a short recommendation directed at lawmakers, using 'should' rather than an open-ended question.

citations.quote: The Senate should reject H.R. 6028.
Lawmakers should reject it, and fast.

observations.description: Brief standalone sentences punctuate longer explanations with a compressed consequence or judgment. Their placement gives the argument a momentary stop before the next section of reasoning.

citations.quote: A.B. 412 ignored those facts, and would have punished some of the most worthwhile projects.
That may seem straightforward. In practice, it’s anything but.

limits: Counts describe this selected evidence, not mandatory quotas.
Zero observations are not a permanent prohibition.
Semantic observations are cited interpretations, not proof of resemblance.
